## A minimal toy {#sec-toy}

{{< question "What does averaging $n$ noisy measurements buy?" >}}

Build the smallest system that shows the phenomenon before touching the real one. Here: each measurement is a standard normal draw, and we average $n$ of them. Over `{python} num(T['reps'])` repetitions, the mean of `{python} num(T['n_ref'])` draws has a spread of `{python} fmt(T['sd'][str(T['n_ref'])], 3)`.

::: {.callout-tip}
Averaging cancels noise because independent errors point in different directions; their sum grows like $\sqrt{n}$, not like $n$.
:::

::: {#def-spread}
## Spread
The spread of an estimator $\hat\mu$ is its standard deviation over repetitions of the experiment, $\operatorname{sd}(\hat\mu)$.
:::

::: {#prp-sqrt}
## The $1/\sqrt{n}$ law
If $x_1, \dots, x_n$ are independent with variance $\sigma^2$, then $\operatorname{sd}(\bar x) = \sigma / \sqrt{n}$.
:::

::: {.proof hint="variances of independent terms add"}
$\operatorname{Var}(\bar x) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_i \operatorname{Var}(x_i) = \sigma^2/n$. Take the square root. ∎
:::

```{python}
#| label: tbl-toy
#| tbl-cap: "Measured spread of the mean against the $1/\\sqrt{n}$ prediction."
#| output: asis
rows = ["| $n$ | measured spread | $1/\\sqrt{n}$ |", "|---:|---:|---:|"]
for n in T["ns"]:
    rows.append(f"| {n} | {fmt(T['sd'][str(n)], 3)} | {fmt(T['theory'][str(n)], 3)} |")
print("\n".join(rows))
```

@tbl-toy shows the measurement within `{python} pct(T['max_rel_dev'])` of the prediction at every $n$ we tried.

::: {#exm-halve}
## Halving the noise
To halve the spread of a mean of `{python} num(T['n_ref'])` draws, take `{python} num(T['n_half'])`: the measured ratio of the two spreads is `{python} fmt(T['ratio_ref_half'], 2)`.
:::

{{< quiz q="Starting from $n$ = `{python} num(T['n_ref'])`, how many draws per mean halve the spread?" a="`{python} num(T['n_half'])`. By @prp-sqrt the spread scales as $1/\sqrt{n}$, so halving it takes four times as many draws; the simulation measures a ratio of `{python} fmt(T['ratio_ref_half'], 2)`." >}}

{{< principle n="1" >}}
Build the smallest system in which the effect appears, and check the formula against it before trusting either.
{{< /principle >}}

{{< takeaway >}}
Noise falls as $1/\sqrt{n}$, so each halving costs four times the data. The next section asks what the paper's system adds to this picture.
{{< /takeaway >}}

## The real system {#sec-real}

{{< question "What does the paper's setting change?" >}}

Carry the toy over to the paper's system, and say exactly where the analogy breaks. Every claim about the paper points to a table, figure or page [@student1908, p. 1].

::: {#alg-check}
## How to test the claim
State the procedure: the data, the comparison, the number that would refute the claim.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the law fails"}
The draws must be independent. Correlated errors do not cancel, and the spread stops falling.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="To verify"}
A figure that could not be checked against the paper or its supplement is marked here, and the pull request lists it.
:::

{{< fold title="Code" hint="the simulation behind the table" >}}
```python
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
means = rng.standard_normal((REPS, n)).mean(axis=1)
sd = means.std(ddof=1)
```
{{< /fold >}}
